lesson.title: A New Kind of Tax: The Townshend Acts and the Road Toward Boston
lesson.summary: After the Stamp Act's repeal, Parliament tried a new approach in 1767 with the Townshend Acts, taxing imported goods rather than domestic activity, but colonists rejected the distinction and the resulting conflict helped set the stage for the Boston Massacre.
lesson.body:
The repeal of the Stamp Act in 1766 left Britain's underlying financial problem unsolved. The government still needed revenue from the colonies, and it still needed a way to pay for administering and defending its expanded North American territory. Charles Townshend, serving as Chancellor of the Exchequer, the official in charge of the treasury, believed he had found a solution that would avoid the backlash of the Stamp Act crisis. Since colonists had objected specifically to what they called an internal tax on their own domestic paper and documents, Townshend proposed a set of duties on goods imported into the colonies from Britain, including glass, lead, paint, paper, and tea, reasoning that colonists had long accepted Parliament's authority to regulate external trade through measures like the Navigation Acts and might accept these new duties on the same grounds.

Parliament passed the Townshend Acts in 1767, and the plan's central assumption quickly proved wrong. Colonial leaders, having spent the Stamp Act crisis building the argument that only their own elected assemblies could tax them for revenue, saw no meaningful difference between an internal tax and an external duty imposed specifically to raise money rather than merely to regulate trade. The Pennsylvania lawyer John Dickinson made this case forcefully in a widely read series of essays published in 1767 and 1768 titled Letters from a Farmer in Pennsylvania, arguing that any parliamentary tax designed purely to generate revenue, whatever form it took, violated the colonists' right to tax themselves through their own representatives.

The Townshend Acts alarmed colonists for another reason as well. The revenue raised was earmarked in part to pay the salaries of royal governors and judges, officials who had previously depended on colonial assemblies to approve their pay. That dependence had given assemblies real leverage over royal officials, and colonists worried that paying salaries directly from London would make governors and judges answerable only to the crown, a direct threat to the tradition of self government built up through bodies like the House of Burgesses and colonial assemblies elsewhere. The Acts also created a new American Board of Customs Commissioners and expanded vice admiralty courts to enforce trade laws more aggressively, deepening colonial resentment of British interference.

Colonists responded with a renewed wave of boycotts of British imports, organized in cities up and down the coast, alongside petitions similar to the resistance that had defeated the Stamp Act. Tensions ran especially high in Boston, where customs officials faced open defiance bitter enough that British troops were sent to occupy the city starting in 1768 to support customs enforcement, a military presence colonists deeply resented in what they considered their own peaceful city.

Facing another effective boycott and pressure from British merchants, Parliament repealed most of the Townshend duties in 1770, keeping only the tax on tea, largely as a symbolic assertion that it still held authority to tax the colonies. By then the occupation of Boston had already produced tragedy: in March 1770, tensions between soldiers and a crowd of colonists boiled over into violence in the event known as the Boston Massacre, in which British soldiers fired into the crowd and killed several colonists. The remaining tax on tea would stay a lingering irritant, setting the stage for the next major confrontation between Britain and its colonies, over tea itself.
